text:
Sila, an advanced battery technology company, announced it has secured $300 million in a private equity round led by Atreides Management, and Sutter Hill Ventures. The round is joined by 8VC, Bessemer Venture Partners, Matrix Partners, funds and accounts advised by T. Rowe Price Associates, Inc, and other existing and new investors. The raise will accelerate U.S. production of Sila’s silicon-carbon (Si/C) anode technology, Titan Silicon® and support a planned Phase 2 expansion at Sila’s plant in Moses Lake, Washington.

The United States cannot rely on foreign supply chains for the materials that power the country’s economy and national security. China controls the battery anode mineral supply chain, with more than 90% of anode material processing and over 80% of global battery cell production, leaving American manufacturers of critical technologies – from drones to sensors to electric vehicles – exposed to single points of failure. A trade dispute, an export restriction, or a supply disruption could stall production across multiple critical technologies at once.

Sila’s team pioneered the modern silicon-carbon (Si/C) anode, a breakthrough technology that delivers 20-40% higher energy density than traditional graphite, enabling batteries that are smaller, lighter, and capable of ultra-fast charging. By pairing American intellectual property with gigascale manufacturing in the United States, Sila is building the blueprint for supply chain security of critical technology.

“This funding allows us to further scale our operations and deliver on the promise of American innovation, strengthen the foundation of our domestic manufacturing capabilities and ensure that critical industries have a secure and reliable supply of advanced batteries,” said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila Co-Founder and CEO.

Sila completed construction and began operations at Moses Lake in fall 2025 and is currently ramping production. Spanning a 160-acre site, Sila’s Moses Lake facility is first-of-a-kind silicon anode plant engineered for scale and designed to expand from its initial 2 GWh of Phase 1 capacity to as much as 250 GWh over the next five years, which would make it the largest anode production facility in the world. As production ramps up, Sila expects the facility to create hundreds of good-paying American jobs, supporting workers, families, and the local economy in Washington State.

“Sila’s transition from a groundbreaking material science inventor to a gigascale manufacturing company is a masterclass in American operational discipline,” commented Vic Miller, Sutter Hill Ventures. “We have watched them translate laboratory breakthroughs into reality, proving that the leap from the lab to the factory floor is not only essential, but achievable in the United States with the right technology and team.”

text:
Your morning catch-up: Californians refuse to give up their gas cars, this SoCal heat wave could be hottest of the year and more big stories

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred

In September 2020, California was burning.

Deadly wildfires scorched a record-breaking swath of the state. Californians suffered from terrible air quality, struggling to breathe amid the COVID-19 pandemic as a sooty plume blotted out the sun. On Sept. 13, The Times published a striking Sunday front-page banner headline: “California’s climate apocalypse.”

In the midst of that chaos, Gov. Gavin Newsom, citing the urgent need to address the climate crisis and cut air pollution, issued an executive order banning the sale of new gasoline-powered cars by 2035.

Polling in the summer of 2021 by the Public Policy Institute of California showed an even split: 49% of Californians supported the plan. And 49% opposed it.

Now, most Californians have soured on it.

A new statewide PPIC poll released this month showed that 66% of Californians now oppose Newsom’s edict, which directed the state Air Resources Board to come up with a plan to require 100% of new cars and light trucks sold in the state by 2035 to be zero-emission.

The air resources board approved such a plan in 2022, with Newsom saying: “It’s ambitious. It’s innovative. It’s the action we must take if we’re serious about leaving this planet better off for future generations.”

Today, per the PPIC poll, most Republicans (91%) and independents (69%) oppose Newsom’s order. Democrats are evenly split.

Opposition is especially high in inland areas such as the pollution-ridden Central Valley, where 74% opposed the order. The highest support came from the Los Angeles region, with 40% in favor (and 59% opposed).

People are worried about charges, both financial and electric.

Amid the spiraling cost of essentials in America — housing, healthcare, child care, gas, utilities, groceries — many simply cannot afford to buy electric vehicles, which typically cost more than fossil-fueled cars.

And in California, my colleague George Skelton reported, residents are not convinced there will be enough charging stations to handle a huge surge in electric vehicles, even though the state now has more than 200,000 public and shared charging stations, plus 800,000 chargers in homes.

The PPIC poll, per Skelton, found “plenty of contradiction and hypocrisy in the divided minds of Californians,” who “strongly favor fighting climate change — at least in concept — until it adversely affects them directly.”

On the other hand, most Californians (62%) favor California’s ambitious law requiring all electricity to come from renewable sources by 2045, per the poll. But fewer than 4 in 10 said they were willing to pay extra for clean energy.

PPIC polling director Mark Baldassare, who owns an electric vehicle, told Skelton he was struck by “the disconnect between what people support in policies and what they’re prepared to do.”

“Two things are going on in California now,” he added. “People have their long-standing concerns about the environment. But they also have immediate concerns about affordability.”

A new rebate is coming for EVs, which make up a solid chunk of sales.

Nearly a year after the expiration of a $7,500 federal tax incentive for new electric vehicles and $4,000 on used ones, Newsom, in his final state budget as governor, allocated $135 million to provide incentives for new and used EVs.

Eligible buyers will receive $3,500 off new EVs and $1,750 off used ones. Unlike the federal tax credits that expired in September, the incentives offer an instant discount and don’t require buyers to apply for credit later. The state and auto manufacturers will split the cost of the incentives.

California leads the country in EV sales, though the PPIC poll shows mixed views about them, with 12% of residents saying they own one and 33% say they have seriously considered purchasing one — and 54% saying they had not considered buying one.

The governor’s press office in an email declined to comment on the PPIC survey, saying it does not typically comment on polls.

In a news release Monday, Newsom said Californians purchased 86,857 new zero-emission vehicles in the second quarter of 2026, representing 19% of new car sales. Demand for such vehicles, the governor’s office said, grew as gasoline prices skyrocketed amid the war with Iran.

“While Donald Trump makes Americans pay the bill for his Iran war at the pump, California is giving families the freedom to choose a cheaper way forward by going electric,” Newsom said in the statement, adding that “we built the largest electric car market in America, and we’re not stopping now.”

Today’s top stories

This SoCal heat wave could be the hottest of the year

Southern California is bracing for its hottest stretch of the year, with triple-digit temperatures and stifling humidity forecast from Tuesday through Monday across much of the region.

Exacerbating the misery will be the lack of cooling temperatures overnight. The L.A. Basin may see low temperatures of only about 70 degrees.

Paramount-Warner Bros. deal on hold after court ruling

A federal judge ruled that the proposed merger “raises serious questions” about whether the blockbuster $111-billion deal violates U.S. antitrust law.

The ruling was anticipated, but it dealt a blow to tech scion David Ellison’s efforts to quickly finalize his massive acquisition, which has the support of President Trump.

New evidence in brutal killing of teen set to come to light

A preliminary hearing in the murder and sexual assault case against David Anthony Burke, a singer who performs under the stage name D4vd, is set to begin Tuesday.

Burke is accused of killing 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez and dismembering her body at his Hollywood Hills home.

What else is going on

UC San Diego illegally uses race in admissions, Trump’s Justice Department alleges.

Sunset Boulevard remains closed as ruptured trunk line repairs continue “into this week.”

E-bike injuries are increasing rapidly in California. Many hurt are 14 or younger, a study finds.

Cyclosporiasis cases climb and the probe into Taylor Farms produce continues after a false positive.

California fights the Trump administration, again, over Santa Barbara oil pipeline: The coast is “not for sale.”

A father-son duo kidnapped U.S. Forest Service workers and held them hostage, the feds say.

Newsom pushes California to crack down on sex trafficking — fast, writes columnist Anita Chabria.

In his latest column, Gustavo Arellano writes about how this World Cup finally taught him to love soccer.

Trump’s transgender-based attack on the CHIPS Act is his most unhinged yet, argues columnist Michael Hiltzik.

This morning’s must-read

Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, a co-founder and longtime leader of Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel, was sentenced to life in U.S. prison by a federal judge in Brooklyn.

For your downtime

Going out

Book crawl: 13 bookstores, one weekend and a $325 grand prize: L.A.’s first book crawl kicks off this weekend.

Staying in

text:
Sustainability-focused investment manager Mirova announced an investment of €150 million (USD$171 million) in renewable energy developer Yanara, aimed at accelerating the development of Yanara’s utility-scale renewable energy portfolio in Australia.

Founded in 2019, and spun off from BrightNight in 2025, Yanara develops, builds, owns and operates utility-scale hybrid renewable energy projects integrating solar, wind and battery energy storage systems (BESS) across the Asia-Pacific region.

Yanara is currently developing a portfolio of more than 5.1 GW of hybrid and dispatchable renewable energy projects across Australia, India and the Philippines, spanning solar, wind and battery energy storage systems (BESS).

The new investment represents Yanara’s first dedicated capital raise in Australia and will support the development of more than 2 GW of multi-technology renewable energy infrastructure across Victoria, New South Wales and Western Australia, the companies noted.

David Delmas, CEO Australia at Yanara, said:

“Australia’s energy market increasingly requires renewable power that is reliable, scalable and available when it is needed most. With Mirova’s support, we can accelerate the development of our gigawatt-scale pipeline and bring more hybrid renewable energy projects to market.”

According to the companies, a significant portion of the investment will be directed towards Yanara’s flagship Mortlake Energy Hub in Victoria, one of Australia’s largest hybrid renewable energy developments. The project will combine 450 MW of solar capacity with a 600 MW/2,400 MWh battery energy storage system to be built in two stages. Once operational, the facility is expected to generate enough clean electricity to power approximately 200,000 homes while avoiding an estimated 880,000 tons of carbon emissions annually. The first phase is preparing to enter construction and is expected to create more than 300 jobs, the companies added.

Raphael Lance, Global Head of Private Assets at Mirova, said:

“Our investment in Yanara reflects Mirova’s long-term commitment to supporting the development of critical energy infrastructure that can accelerate Australia’s transition to a more resilient and low-carbon energy system. We are delighted to partner with an experienced management team and look forward to contributing to the delivery of a high-quality portfolio of flexible renewable energy coupled with BESS assets across the country.”

title: 3 practical steps to ensure the US industrial boom runs on electricity | Utility Dive
description:
As manufacturers modernize facilities and look for ways to manage costs, industrial electrification should be part of the strategy.
It is an opportunity already within the nation’s reach, provided policymakers treat industrial electrification as an economic imperative.
Capturing this opportunity also requires engineers, electricians, contractors, technicians, and plant operators who understand industrial energy systems.
Companies are reassessing supply chains, states are competing for industrial investment, and utilities are planning for a new era of load growth.
Industrial electrification fits each of those conversations, and the path forward does not depend on speculative technology.
text:
American manufacturers are making long-term investments in an increasingly complex environment: fuel prices remain volatile, global competition is intensifying, domestic supply chains are becoming a renewed priority, and the equipment installed today may shape operating costs for decades. In that context, one opportunity deserves more attention: modernizing the heat systems that power American manufacturing.

Industrial heat — the steam and hot water that process food, the thermal systems behind chemicals and paper, and the heat running through countless manufacturing processes — accounts for a substantial share of manufacturers’ energy costs. Most of it still comes from natural gas, leaving manufacturers exposed every time global energy markets move.

As manufacturers modernize facilities and look for ways to manage costs, industrial electrification should be part of the strategy.

Switching a meaningful share of that heat to electricity, through commercially available technologies like industrial heat pumps, electric boilers, and thermal batteries, could unlock roughly $254 billion in investment, generate $471 billion in economic activity, add $185 billion to GDP, and support 1.66 million jobs by 2035, according to new analysis.

Every dollar invested would support approximately $1.85 in total economic activity. These projects do not stop at the factory gate. They ripple through equipment suppliers, construction firms, engineering services, logistics networks, and local communities in manufacturing-heavy states, while also creating growth opportunities in smaller states with industrial assets of their own.

This is not a projection about some distant energy transition. It is an opportunity already within the nation’s reach, provided policymakers treat industrial electrification as an economic imperative.

For manufacturers, electrification means reducing dependence on a fuel whose price swings with global commodity markets. Long-term electricity procurement, on-site generation, efficiency, and flexible operations give manufacturers more ways to manage their energy bills. For companies competing on tight margins, that kind of stability matters for businesses and consumers alike.

For the grid, flexibility matters too. As rising electricity demand puts upward pressure on costs, policymakers should care not only about how much new demand is added, but also about what kind. Industrial facilities that can store heat and shift some energy use to off-peak hours can help reduce stress on the grid and make better use of existing infrastructure. At a moment when affordability is a top concern for regulators and ratepayers alike, that is exactly the kind of new demand the grid needs.

The barriers are real, but they are not primarily technological. Capturing this opportunity requires three practical moves: make electricity pricing work better for industrial customers, help manufacturers finance projects, and build the domestic supply chains and workforce needed to deploy these technologies at scale.

First, electricity pricing needs to better reflect the value some industrial customers can provide to the grid. In many regions, manufacturers that electrify can face charges that make otherwise promising projects harder to justify, even when those projects could help shift demand away from peak hours. Rate design is mostly a state-level issue, but federal policymakers can help by funding demonstrations, sharing best practices, and supporting analysis that shows how flexible industrial demand can benefit both manufacturers and the grid.

Second, manufacturers need tools to manage upfront costs and prepare sites for investment. Replacing industrial heat systems is not a simple equipment swap. It can involve engineering studies, facility retrofits, utility coordination, and planned downtime. Targeted loans, tax incentives, federal-state cost-sharing, technical assistance, and dedicated funding programs can help early projects prove the economics for the next wave. Clear long-term policy signals also give manufacturers confidence to plan investments that may take years to develop and deploy.

Third, America can build more of the equipment itself and the workforce needed to deploy it. As American factories electrify, more of the equipment used to do it can come from American factories. Capturing this opportunity also requires engineers, electricians, contractors, technicians, and plant operators who understand industrial energy systems. Community colleges, apprenticeships, manufacturer partnerships, and practical supports such as transportation, childcare, and flexible training options can help workers move into these roles.

Read More in Building & Transportation Electrification

The political moment is well-suited to this push. Companies are reassessing supply chains, states are competing for industrial investment, and utilities are planning for a new era of load growth. Industrial electrification fits each of those conversations, and the path forward does not depend on speculative technology. The solutions exist. The economic case is documented. What is missing is policy focus.

Competitors abroad are not waiting. Countries in Europe and Asia are investing in industrial electrification, building equipment supply chains, training workers, and positioning themselves to capture manufacturing investment that could otherwise land here. American manufacturers should not lose investment opportunities because other countries offer clearer pathways to modernize industrial energy systems. Keeping that investment here will require better project economics, stronger domestic equipment supply chains, and a workforce ready to deploy these technologies at scale.

America is deciding what kind of industrial economy it wants to build. The answer will not be determined only by which factories are announced or which supply chains are reshored. It will also depend on whether manufacturers can control energy costs, whether the grid can manage new demand affordably, and whether the equipment and workforce behind industrial modernization are built here. Greater energy cost certainty for manufacturers can also help reduce one source of pressure on the cost of food, household goods, and other everyday products.

Industrial electrification belongs in that conversation. If the U.S. wants the next industrial boom to be built here, it needs to modernize not only what factories make but how they are powered.

text:
Mosaic Fertilizer and its subsidiary, Tampa Port Services, have agreed to pay a $103,449.50 federal penalty to settle alleged equipment safety violations linked to an anhydrous ammonia release at their Faustina industrial complex in western St. James Parish.

The settlement follows an Oct. 27, 2025, release of anhydrous ammonia that exposed four contract workers. Two workers received oxygen treatment before returning to work the same day, according to state incident records.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency alleged the companies violated federal chemical safety requirements by failing to maintain equipment to prevent hazardous releases. Under the settlement, Mosaic and Tampa Port neither admitted nor denied the violations but agreed to resolve the case and waived their right to appeal.

According to state records, about 673 pounds of anhydrous ammonia vapor were released when a pressure relief valve opened during maintenance work. The vapor was routed to an emergency flare that was still under construction, allowing it to escape into the air. Workers contained the release within about 30 minutes, and the company said the ammonia did not travel off-site, although employees and contractors sheltered in place.

State regulators allege the release exceeded the facility’s permitted hourly emission limit by more than eight times. Tampa Port later acknowledged the incident was preventable, attributing it to a pressure relief valve that had been set too low.

The October release followed another preventable ammonia release on June 4, 2025, when an estimated 4,436 pounds of anhydrous ammonia escaped after another improperly calibrated relief valve opened prematurely. Both incidents remain part of an ongoing investigation by the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality.

In a statement, Mosaic said it has implemented corrective actions, including additional employee training, maintaining an inventory of critical spare pressure relief valves and strengthening quality control procedures.

The latest settlement marks the second EPA enforcement action involving the companies in just over two years. In January 2024, Mosaic and Tampa Port agreed to pay $217,085 in civil penalties and spend $100,000 on environmental projects in St. James Parish, including installing 11 ammonia air monitors, to resolve earlier allegations involving mechanical integrity and process safety.

title: Provocative New Study Says New Orleans Cannot Be Protected Forever. Is It Time to Plan a Retreat?

text:
New Orleans exists because it bargains with water.

The city pumps it, walls it off, channels it, blesses it, fears it, and dances beside it. For more than three centuries, that uneasy bargain has made life possible on the shifting, sinking sediment of the Mississippi River Delta.

But a provocative new paper argues that the bargain is no longer tenable.

Writing in Nature Sustainability, researchers say southeast Louisiana can expect between 3 and 7 metres (roughly 10 to 23 feet) of eventual relative sea-level rise. At those levels, the shoreline could move more than 100 kilometres inland in parts of the state, leaving New Orleans surrounded by open water or ultimately inundated.

It’s not clear exactly when this will happen. But, given how the climate looks today, the long-term destiny of New Orleans seems to be in great peril.

The Shoreline Is Coming

New Orleans is built on the shifting sediment of the Mississippi River Delta. Much of the city lies at or below sea level, protected by an intricate network of levees, floodwalls and pumps. In 2005, hurricane Katrina exposed the limits of those defenses, but even as billions of dollars have been invested to strengthen them, the threat has also increased. The wetlands that once buffered the city from the Gulf of Mexico are disappearing, the land beneath it is slowly sinking, and climate-driven sea-level rise is steadily tipping the balance against one of the world’s most vulnerable coastal landscapes.

Their paper, led by Tulane University geologist Torbjörn Törnqvist, with researchers from Yale University, Florida State University and Coastal Carolina University, argues that southeast Louisiana has likely crossed a geological threshold. The team analyzed data from the past 125,000 years ago, looking particularly at Ponchatoula Ridge, about 50 kilometers north of the city. This ridge is a remnant shoreline from a period called the Last Interglacial, from 125,000 years ago.

Back then, global temperatures were only modestly warmer than preindustrial levels, but seas stood far higher than today. In southeast Louisiana, the paper estimates that relative sea level reached about 3.1 meters above today’s reference level, and perhaps about 7.5 meters once long-term fault motion and subsidence are accounted for.

So, basically, current conditions are enough to push the Gulf Coast more than 100 kilometers inland. The problem, however, is that they can’t say when that shoreline will arrive.

For Jesse Keenan, a climate adaptation researcher at Tulane University and one of the paper’s authors, that uncertainty is precisely why planning should begin immediately.

“The real question is when and what does it mean to begin to plan a transition of the population, of businesses, of capital,” he said in an interview with NPR. “There is not currently planning by the city or the state to begin this transition.”

What Timeline Are We Looking At?

The timeline might not be clear, but Louisiana doesn’t need to wait for several metres of sea-level rise to experience a radically altered coast.

Since the 1930s, coastal Louisiana has lost more than 5,000 square kilometres of land. The remaining wetlands protect communities by absorbing waves and reducing storm-surge energy, but they are disappearing as the land sinks, sediment supplies decline and seas rise.

One assessment cited in the paper found that losing 75% of the remaining roughly 15,000 square kilometres of coastal wetlands by 2070 is plausible under a middle-of-the-road emissions pathway that the authors describe as close to the current trajectory.

Basically, all watery hell could break loose within a few decades.

Levees, floodwalls, gates and pumps can buy time. After Hurricane Katrina exposed catastrophic weaknesses in the city’s protection system in 2005, billions of dollars went into stronger defences. But those structures must operate in an increasingly hostile landscape as the wetlands outside them disappear.

The silver lining is that the city’s defense systems will slow things down. But that goal of that slowing down is to help with managed relocations.

A Difficult Retreat

Managed relocation means moving to a place safe from the incoming shoreline, while continuing to restore wetlands and maintain flood defenses to buy as much time as possible. In the paper, the authors point to higher ground north of Lake Pontchartrain as one example of a future receiving area that could be developed deliberately instead of growing through crisis-driven migration.

Their concern is that relocation is already happening — but without a plan.

Since Hurricane Katrina, Orleans Parish has lost roughly a quarter of its population. The problem is that hurricanes are only part of the story. Poverty, suburbanization, jobs, housing costs, insurance premiums and family ties all influence whether people stay or leave. Climate pressure acts on top of those existing forces, often making difficult choices even harder.

Families with money and mobility can leave early. Residents with fewer resources may become trapped as insurance costs rise, services decline and property becomes harder to sell.

The paper’s argument isn’t just “abandon New Orleans.” It says Louisiana needs to use the time it still has to make retreat orderly, fair and useful for the entire community.

What Managed Relocation Would Look Like

Coastal restoration still matters a lot. The authors argue that slowing wetland loss could buy precious time for a multi-generational transition.

Managed relocation would be a slow, multigenerational process. It could include directing new housing and infrastructure toward higher ground, helping vulnerable households move voluntarily, discouraging risky new construction and preparing receiving communities before disaster-driven migration overwhelms them.

The researchers believe Louisiana has a rare opportunity.

Because climate-driven depopulation has already begun, the state could become the first place to develop a model for managed relocation before disaster forces it. If successful, that blueprint could eventually be used by coastal communities around the world facing the same dilemma.

The proposal has already sparked fierce criticism. Business leaders and state officials argue the paper is overly pessimistic and risks discouraging investment by discussing relocation without a clear timetable. They contend New Orleans has repeatedly adapted and should continue investing in protection rather than talking about retreat.

The authors acknowledge the politics are difficult, especially because they don’t have a clear timeline. But managed relocation or not, with the current climate heating trends, it seems unlikely that New Orleans will remain protected forever.

The future may not arrive as one dramatic moment when the Gulf suddenly crosses a line. It may come through repeated storms, rising costs, shrinking communities and thousands of individual decisions to leave.

The choice, the paper argues, is whether that transition is planned fairly — or dictated by the next disaster.

title: Adani–Dioxycle partnership to advance low-carbon chemical manufacturing
description:
Adani Enterprises Ltd (AEL), the flagship company of the Adani Group, and Dioxycle, a French clean-technology company specializing in chemical manufacturing, have announced a long-term partnership to develop and scale low-carbon chemical production in India.
The partnership combines Dioxycle's electrically driven chemical manufacturing technology with Adani Group's clean-energy capabilities, infrastructure platform and project execution expertise to create a new model for sustainable and cost-competitive chemical production.
This partnership with Dioxycle is a testament to how strategic industrial synergies can turn carbon liabilities into sustainable, cost-effective economic assets,” said Mr. Jeet Adani, Director, Adani Group.
India offers a unique combination of renewable energy, manufacturing capability, and ambition.
Together with Adani, we aim to build a competitive and scalable model for low-carbon chemical production," said Dr. Sarah Lamaison, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Co-Founder of Dioxycle.
text:
Adani Enterprises Ltd (AEL), the flagship company of the Adani Group, and Dioxycle, a French clean-technology company specializing in chemical manufacturing, have announced a long-term partnership to develop and scale low-carbon chemical production in India.

The initiative will begin with a pilot facility at an Adani Group’s site to produce formic acid using captured carbon dioxide and renewable electricity. Following successful validation, the partners plan to scale the technology for commercial manufacturing.

Formic acid and its derivatives are widely used across industries including textiles, agriculture and manufacturing. The project aims to demonstrate how captured carbon emissions can be converted into valuable products using clean energy.

The partnership combines Dioxycle's electrically driven chemical manufacturing technology with Adani Group's clean-energy capabilities, infrastructure platform and project execution expertise to create a new model for sustainable and cost-competitive chemical production.

“We are proud to pilot India's first formic acid production facility powered entirely by renewable electricity and captured carbon. This partnership with Dioxycle is a testament to how strategic industrial synergies can turn carbon liabilities into sustainable, cost-effective economic assets,” said Mr. Jeet Adani, Director, Adani Group.

"This partnership demonstrates how clean technology and industrial scale can come together to reshape how essential chemicals are produced. India offers a unique combination of renewable energy, manufacturing capability, and ambition. title: Miliband has been relentlessly attacked for net zero; what will happen now? - The Guardian
description:
Unfailingly upbeat, with a simple message that was understandable to voters, he had a clear mission – to decarbonise the UK’s power sector by 2030 – that was seen to be progressing fast.
Miliband may be personally disappointed if Burnham does this, having previously described Rosebank as “climate vandalism”.
Ami McCarthy, the head of politics at Greenpeace UK, points to the deep pockets of vested interests and the might of the fossil fuel industry.
In fact, energy prices would have been much higher without Miliband’s actions.
If he had been made chancellor, as was rumoured at one point, Miliband could have been expected to tackle this.
text:
“Whenever the Labour party feels a bit sad,” according to one close observer of the current government, speaking some months ago, “they wheel out Ed Miliband to talk about rooftop solar.”

It might not have been literally true, but it often felt during Keir Starmer’s premiership as if energy secretary Miliband brought the sun. Unfailingly upbeat, with a simple message that was understandable to voters, he had a clear mission – to decarbonise the UK’s power sector by 2030 – that was seen to be progressing fast.

While the Treasury struggled with feeble growth and political gaffes such as the winter fuel payments, the NHS was disrupted by doctors’ strikes, and education laboured under dilapidated schools and discouraged teachers, Miliband’s department seemed to get stuff done at an unusual rate.

“His detractors won’t like to admit it, but Miliband has been the most successful minister under the Starmer administration,” says Ed Matthew, the UK director at the E3G thinktank. “Perhaps that is why they have attacked him so viciously.”

Rightwing media publications have published frequent editorials attacking Miliband, labelling him a “net-zero zealot” with a “messianic” devotion to climate action. Even as three intense heatwaves struck this summer and firefighters battled wildfires across the country, the calls for more drilling for the fossil fuels that are supercharging extreme weather got louder.

The fossil fuel industry, along with the Conservatives, Reform UK and sections of the Labour party, has been lobbying Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, for the Jackdaw gasfield, east of Aberdeen, and Rosebank, an oilfield west of Shetland, to be given the go-ahead. Media reports suggested Burnham was preparing to announce new drilling in the North Sea shortly after entering No 10.

Miliband may be personally disappointed if Burnham does this, having previously described Rosebank as “climate vandalism”. Miliband was also behind the push to have no new licences as a manifesto commitment.

But giving the go-ahead to Jackdaw or Rosebank would not technically breach the manifesto ban, which left a loophole for the issue of licences that were already within the planning system.

For some months, it has been clear that some such compromise might be demanded and the ground has been prepared. One close civil society observer, who did not wish to be named, said: “It is not what we wanted, but we have to get on with the rest of what’s needed.”

That bigger picture has been described as “an energy revolution”, the trajectory of which is unstoppable, whatever the changing political weather.

Matthew said: “Setting the 2030 clean power target was less about meeting the target than setting turbo boosters under the clean economy to get lift-off – which [Miliband] has achieved with record levels of renewables contracts and reforms to massively speed up deployment. This is critical to economic growth, reindustrialisation, energy security and, yes, bringing down bills. This is an energy revolution which is now inevitable and no amount of grumbling by the politicians and media barons funded by fossil fuel interests can reverse it.”

Now Miliband has moved beyond the energy department to the Foreign Office. He has always had an eye on the global aspects of this transition, acting as a powerful voice at climate summits and arguing for change. He will bring his climate knowledge and undoubted energies to bear on this role.

After all, within 72 hours of taking office in the energy department in July 2024, Miliband had lifted the ban on onshore windfarms and begun the process of consenting offshore windfarms and solar farms, while reforming a previously chaotic queue for grid connections. Auctions for low-carbon generation secured enough to supply about 23m homes, while the warm homes plan to install insulation, heat pumps and clean energy should lift about 1 million families out of fuel poverty. A new nuclear programme for small modular reactors is also under way.

Last month, the government announced that the private sector had committed about £100bn to the UK’s clean technology sector. Alongside that, there is a plan to support 400,000 people into low-carbon jobs – more than double the number employed in the rapidly declining North Sea basin.

It is curious why Miliband, a former Labour leader who lost to the Conservatives in 2015, has also been the target of unrelenting internal negative briefing. Some of it comes from his long history, stretching back to his role as one of former prime minister Gordon Brown’s proteges in the early 2000s. But other factions also pitched in.

He is popular with Labour members, which may irk some. “At a time when lots of people want to say ‘a plague on all your houses’ about politicians, Miliband stands out as a rare example of someone who’s actually made a difference,” says Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts. “So much of that has down been down to his genuine leadership and having a real sense of purpose and vision behind it, and determination to get on with it, even when you have extraordinarily ridiculous attacks from some parts of the political spectrum.”

Attacks on Miliband from other political parties have been equally vituperative: he has been behind only Starmer, and perhaps the chancellor, Rachel Reeves, as one of the key targets of Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader. Nigel Farage and his Reform party have vowed to make net zero “the next Brexit”. And two large unions, Unite and the GMB, launched a fierce campaign against his proposed elevation to chancellor of the exchequer, though other unions backed him.

Ami McCarthy, the head of politics at Greenpeace UK, points to the deep pockets of vested interests and the might of the fossil fuel industry. “It’s no surprise that an agenda which challenges the profits of big oil has made him the target of coordinated smears by the industry and its allies, including the latest attacks we’ve seen this month,” they say.

Businesses, led by the CBI, pointed out that the UK’s high energy prices – about 45% above the G7 median – were damaging businesses and dampening growth, as well as raising the cost of living.

But as the CBI has made clear, net zero is not the culprit. In fact, energy prices would have been much higher without Miliband’s actions. His reforms add up to about £150 off bills for the average household, while about 6 million families on low incomes will gain about £150 more through the warm homes discount.

The problem is that people are not seeing the result in their pockets, because fossil fuel prices have risen even faster, through the compound shocks of the Ukraine invasion and the Iran war, which have sent gas and oil prices soaring. Added to this are the rules Labour inherited governing the UK’s privatised power market, which mean that the price of electricity is set by gas-fired power stations, which can be highly profitable for them but disastrous for consumers.

Miliband has been trying to wean the UK off fossil fuels, to cheap renewable energy. This will require more investment, particularly in the grid. And the government is intent on decoupling gas and electricity prices, but this is proving a tough and slow process.

If he had been made chancellor, as was rumoured at one point, Miliband could have been expected to tackle this. But John Healey, previously the defence secretary, may have less enthusiasm for that fight.

His move to the Foreign Office will prevent Miliband from following through on this project, and it remains to be seen whether his replacement, Miatta Fahnbulleh, will continue it with such enthusiasm. But it will cheer many of his international allies; the fight to limit the climate crisis is a global one, and the US departure from the field, coupled with uncertainty in Europe, and China and India’s flirtations with Russia, have left a leadership vacuum.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, says: “On the international stage, Miliband is seen as someone who understands that ambitious climate action and economic renewal can go hand in hand. Climate diplomacy is built on relationships, trust and persistence, and countries notice when senior ministers are prepared to engage directly. Putting [him] at the heart of government would send a positive signal to the rest of the world.”

Teresa Ribera, a vice-president of the European Commission responsible for green transition, has been a close ally since Miliband began his first stint as energy secretary in 2008. “He is, by some distance, one of the most skilful and respected negotiators I have ever worked with, and one of the most honest and principled politicians I know. He commands respect in international institutions and among the world’s most influential governments, but equally among developing countries, workers, scientists and business and civil society leaders,” she told the Guardian.

text:
DETROIT — General Motors will launch new gas-powered Cadillac vehicles beginning next spring as the automaker continues to shift gears away from all-electric vehicles.

GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday that the next-generation Cadillacs will include new versions of the company's CT5 sedan, outdated XT5 midsize SUV and discontinued three-row XT6 SUV.

"Starting next spring and continuing into 2028, we will begin launching the next generation of Cadillac ICE [internal combustion engine] vehicles," Barra said during the company's second-quarter earnings call. She said the vehicles will be in addition to Cadillac's current all-electric crossovers and Escalade SUV.

The new product announcements add to GM's pullback in EVs. The automaker had planned for Cadillac to exclusively sell electric vehicles by the end of this decade. The company also has walked back EV plans for other brands and increased gas-powered engine production, including V-8 offerings.

GM has recorded $10.9 billion in EV-related charges since the second half of last year after slower-than-expected electric vehicle adoption as well as U.S. regulatory changes easing emissions standards and eliminating support for EVs.

Barra reiterated that GM's plans include "onshoring significant manufacturing" for the Detroit automaker beginning next year, in part by expanding production of its full-size SUVs to a Michigan plant that was previously slated to build EVs.

The full-size SUVs — Escalade, Chevy Tahoe and Suburban, and GMC Yukon and Yukon XL — are currently exclusively produced at the company's Arlington Assembly plant in Texas.

text:
The US charging network 2.0—The evolution of a revolution: Part 3

» Read part 1 here: How the biggest US EV charging networks got their starts

» Read part 2 here: How government helped build America’s EV charging market

The US charging landscape is still evolving quickly. Some operators are downsizing or exiting, others are winning major subsidies or loan guarantees, and a new class of competitors—from travel centers to automaker-backed ventures—is trying to scale into the gap.

The shakeout continues

During the past two years, the charging network landscape continued its evolution as several operators shuttered or retreated due to challenging economics. In 2024, European companies Engie and Enel X both left the US market after trying to leverage their domestic charging experience. In December 2024, Shell announced it would stop supporting the charging software it had licensed to other companies and instead focus on managing chargers at its own retail locations. In August 2025, Shell scaled back further by halting operations of the Volta network of 2,000 chargers that it had acquired in 2023. In November, Shell sold portions of the Volta network to JOLT, an international operator of chargers and digital media.

Conversely, EVgo received a major boost when it landed a $1.25 billion DOE loan guarantee in December 2024 to expand its public fast-charging footprint nationwide. Overall, the number of fast chargers installed across the country continued to swell in 2025, with nearly 1,500 stations added in the second and third quarters according to Paren. Tesla far outpaced every other network in growth, controlling nearly 45% of all charging ports added in Q3.

The largest charging networks are also busily building stations with NEVI support. According to the EVStates Clearinghouse awards dashboard, as of April 2026, Tesla, EVgo, Electrify America, Blink and ChargePoint have collectively been awarded $67.5 million in NEVI funds to build 834 charging ports—an average cost to taxpayers of $67,500 per port. Newer competitors are also pursuing those awards aggressively. Two of the biggest beneficiaries are convenience-store operators Love’s Travel Stops & Country Stores and Pilot Travel Centers, which together plan to install nearly 700 charging ports. Love’s is developing locations in partnership with ChargePoint, while Pilot works with EVgo and other networks.

Privately held Francis Energy, founded in 2015, has received more than $105 million in NEVI funds—more than any other company—and operates 143 charging locations across nine states. EVGateway, launched in 2017, ranks as the fifth-largest NEVI recipient at roughly $25 million and says it has a network of 2,500 stations.

A charging network backed by a group of automakers has also emerged as a formidable competitor. OEMs have long been skeptical that the private market would keep up with EV sales while delivering a high-quality charging experience, and in July 2023 BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes and Stellantis announced plans to create a fast-charging network in the US and Canada. The venture, later named IONNA, was joined by Toyota a year later and intends to operate 30,000 chargers. IONNA prioritized convenience-store locations and struck deals with Sheetz, Wawa and Casey’s. By March of 2026 Ionna has 100 locations in operation and had won $3.3 million in NEVI funds. It could remain independent, or eventually become an acquirer itself.

In addition to federal incentives that may soon disappear, charging networks can lower upfront costs through state, municipal and utility programs. California’s CALeVIP remains the largest example, with other notable programs in New Jersey and New York.

Why this matters: The market is not simply growing, it is churning. Some players are exiting, some are consolidating, and others are using public support or strategic partnerships to try to gain enough scale to survive.

Reliability is improving, but uptime still rules

Maintaining functioning charging stations—not only to keep the door to revenue ajar, but also to reduce EV owner angst—continues to be challenging. The industry has made progress in reliability, usually measured in uptime, the percentage of time a charger is ready for use, but there is still ample room for improvement. According to a 2025 JD Power survey of public charging, the percentage of visits in which EV drivers could not get any power fell to its lowest level in four years, a sign that reliability and customer experience are steadily improving.

Poor uptime makes the already difficult task of achieving strong utilization and profitability even harder, according to Wayne Killen, former Director of Charging Infrastructure Planning and Business Development at Electrify America. If chargers can deliver power around 20% of the time, then the promised land of profitability could be reached. Any time a charger is offline beyond normal maintenance and upkeep reduces revenue potential, he said.

Pat (Pasquale) Romano, who led ChargePoint for nearly 13 years, likewise said he has seen progress in both charging reliability and the underlying power-delivery technology. “I think charging technology development is going well,” he said. “There is no technology deficit.”

Why this matters: A charging site can only earn money when it is energized, functional and trusted. Reliability is not just a customer-experience metric, it is the first gate to utilization and therefore to profitability.

The economics problem—and the equity paradox

Profitability remains elusive for charging network operators. The three largest publicly traded charging companies—Blink, ChargePoint and EVgo—posted combined net losses of more than $600 million in 2024, based on their income statements. Tesla’s charging profitability is harder to isolate because it sits inside a much broader business. All three pure-play charging companies also saw their stock prices slide in 2025.

Network profitability is constrained by both how much traffic comes to a station and the upper limit of the fees drivers are willing to pay. The industry’s conventional wisdom has long held that a charge cannot cost more per mile than filling a gas tank, but that view is softening. DC fast charging that exceeds the cost of gasoline can be tolerated for occasional long-distance trips as long as it is not excessive and as long as drivers look at their total cost of driving electric. If most charging (estimated at up to 80%) happens cheaply at home—where costs can be less than 12 cents per kWh—then using public infrastructure for the remaining 20% can still make economic sense. Level 2 charging, better suited for overnight or other long dwell times, costs more than residential charging but less than gasoline. According to Stable Auto, the average cost of Level 2 charging in summer 2025 was 25 cents per kWh and fast charging was 47 cents per kWh.

Romano said infrequent fast charging, used to complement less-expensive home and workplace charging, may cost more than gasoline but is acceptable because for drivers it “has little impact on their overall fuel bill.”

High utilization is needed to pay back the initial cost—often hundreds of thousands of dollars—to equip and energize a charging station, while also offsetting the ongoing cost of electricity. Yet wide utilization differences between seemingly similar sites continue to mystify network operators. Charging networks are constrained by the “glass ceiling of how many EVs are on the road” in an area, according to Romano. Third-party tools that model likely traffic at a charging location can reduce some of the guesswork, but they cannot conjure demand that is not there.

Some stations are necessary even though they may never make money. Rural locations and low-EV-density corridors are essential to enable travel, but they are unlikely to ever be profitable on their own. Ben Prochazka, the Executive Director of the Electrification Coalition, argues that the cost of these less-frequented locations should be socialized across the broader network, much as utilities provide power in less densely populated areas.

The expansion of the EV market to include a more diverse audience can boost utilization, but it also presents a paradox. Drivers who cannot charge at home and rely on public charging are often more price-sensitive and less able to pay premium fast-charging fees. According to a 2025 Federal Reserve report on housing and household well-being, 85% of families making more than $100,000 own their homes, while well under half of families making under $100,000 do. That homeownership gap matters because it often determines whether a driver has access to low-cost home charging. Developing discounted rates or incentives for lower-income EV drivers, including high-mileage rideshare drivers, could help create the utilization that operators crave without pushing away the customers most dependent on public infrastructure.

Why this matters: The hard part was never just installing chargers. It was building a business that can tolerate high capital costs, uneven traffic, power costs, rural obligations, and customers whose willingness to pay is constrained by the very economics that make public charging necessary.

Next in the series: The economics of public charging are still tough, but the industry is already starting to adapt. In Part 4, we look at how charging networks are evolving to become more reliable, better utilized and more financially durable.

title: As private equity creeps into Louisiana utilities, ratepayers face an uphill battle
authors: Camden Doherty, The Current, Camden Doherty, The Current, Elise Plunk, Wesley Muller, Greg LaRose
description:
Across the room sit representatives from the Louisiana Public Service Commission and Magnolia Water, accompanied by a squadron of attorneys.
Most customers now pay more than $73 a month for sewer service, along with a starting water rate of $44.
By comparison, the statewide average is $56 for sewer service and a $19 starting water rate.
Like the water system serving the town of Kilian, which is among the for-profit utility provider’s most recent acquisitions.
“The residents that have Magnolia Water cannot deal with another ‘moderate’ rate hike,” she told the sitting commissioners this June.
text:
This report was first published by The Current, a nonprofit news organization serving Lafayette and South Louisiana.

Cindy Case-Brown and Connie Norris sit on the far side of the nearly empty hearing room in the Galvez Building in Baton Rouge, several small stacks of documents and binders spread out before them. Across the room sit representatives from the Louisiana Public Service Commission and Magnolia Water, accompanied by a squadron of attorneys.

The two Magnolia customers traveled from the Northshore to the state capital to oppose a plan that would allow the private equity-backed company to continue to increase water and sewer rates annually. In recent years, Magnolia has bought up utility systems across the state, becoming one of Louisiana’s largest water and sewer providers.

Like many Louisiana residents, Case-Brown and Norris have seen their utility rates soar since Magnolia took over their local system. Unlike most, they dove headfirst into the regulatory muck.

It has been an uphill battle since day one.

“I had very little knowledge of what was going on and how the system worked,” says Norris, who eventually became an intervenor in one of Magnolia’s repeated requests to the LPSC for permission to raise its rates on customers like herself.

The process is similar to court proceedings — only Norris and fellow Magnolia customers don’t have anyone to represent them but themselves.

According to LPSC records, Magnolia now provides sewer to more than 82,000 customers across the state and water to an additional 79,000 connections. The company continues to expand through acquisitions.

Since Magnolia started expanding in 2019, the company has increased utility rates for its customers nearly every year, making its sewer rates the highest in the state. Residents in Lafayette’s Quail Hollow neighborhood saw sewer rate hikes as high as 200%. Most customers now pay more than $73 a month for sewer service, along with a starting water rate of $44. By comparison, the statewide average is $56 for sewer service and a $19 starting water rate.

Fighting those increases, as Case-Brown and Norris set out to do, is difficult.

The LPSC, the state body in charge of regulating and approving rate increases by private companies like Magnolia, has a tendency to approve them without much discussion, in part because it sees its role as ensuring that those companies have the financial wherewithal to continue operations and comply with federal and state regulations.

“The LPSC is responsible for ensuring that utilities are able to generate enough funds to maintain compliance with these regulatory agencies,” writes LPSC staff in its Magnolia hearing filings.

Meanwhile, Magnolia has done everything in its power to make intervention as painful as possible, arguing that ratepayers like Case-Brown and Norris should have to sign non-disclosure agreements to see the financial data the company used to justify its rate increases, and even requesting insight into their personal finances and medical records in return.

Magnolia did not respond to any requests for comment by The Current for this story. All quotes from Magnolia representatives come from public hearings and filings.

The company argues it needs to raise rates in order to fix the many old systems it has taken over that had fallen into disrepair under previous ownership.

Higher operating costs, shrinking populations and lack of government support have left many small towns with failing systems and no money to hire engineers to fix the deficiencies.

According to a 2020 report from the American Society of Civil Engineers, spending on capital improvements to water infrastructure in 2019 at the local, state and federal levels totaled only $48 billion.

This fell $81 billion short of the $129 billion ASCE estimates is needed to effectively modernize the system. At the same time, ASCE gave water systems across the country a D rating, meaning improvements are needed for failing systems now.

Those are exactly the kinds of systems Magnolia and its parent company have taken over in Louisiana and beyond.

Like the water system serving the town of Kilian, which is among the for-profit utility provider’s most recent acquisitions.

Until 2026, the town’s water system consistently received a D or F rating from the Louisiana Department of Health.

The town tried, and failed, to drag itself out. “We were going to go bankrupt. Hiring these engineering firms or these contractors is incredibly expensive,” says Mayor Caleb Atwell of the repairs needed to keep Killian’s water drinkable.

Manganese and iron concentrations are high in the area’s groundwater, and improper filtration makes the water coming out of the tap less than appetizing.

“You’re turning on your sink, and it looks like gumbo is coming out,” says Atwell. “And not the good kind of gumbo. We’re talking tomato.”

Atwell was elected mayor in 2025. By that time, the town’s water system had already been in receivership, meaning the state had taken ownership of the system due to the persistently bad ratings. Meanwhile, residents paid less than $30 for water service a month, nowhere near enough to generate the funds for necessary repairs, he argues.

“People really don’t care too much about the pipes that are in the ground, until they start breaking,” says Atwell. “You’re only charging people $28 a month, great, but you can’t put in the dollars that it takes to upgrade.”

After over a year in receivership, the Louisiana Department of Health came to Killian with an ultimatum: Sell the system to Magnolia or fight the court-ordered sale of the system.

“We really didn’t have an option but to go with Magnolia,” says Atwell.

Magnolia Founder and CEO Josiah Cox agrees. “I believe we’re the only entity that’s kind of capable or willing to step into that situation,” he told the LPSC in a February hearing.

But unlike a public utility like Lafayette Utilities System and many of the water and sewage districts it takes over, Magnolia is backed by private investors and expected to turn a profit for those shareholders.

Magnolia’s most recent rate plan approved by the LPSC ensures customer rates provide a 9% to 10% financial return for Magnolia, on top of the tens of millions in expenses the company already recoups from acquiring and operating systems.

According to its application for rate increases in 2025, Magnolia owed more than $37.5 million to its parent company, funds that have been used to support the company’s expansion across the state. Continued expansion, Cox argues, is necessary for the company’s business model to function, something he says will bring down rates in the long run.

“We can buy equipment that smaller utilities couldn’t afford on their own, because we’re managing multiple utilities across a larger footprint,” Cox said in the February hearing.

Assessing the validity of that claim and arguing against it, if necessary, requires a level of expertise that many ratepayers — and even regulators — lack, says Jackson Voss, a law student working for the Alliance for Affordable Energy, a nonprofit that intervenes in electrical rate cases on behalf of ratepayers.

“Doing that requires very active regulation and very active balancing of the interests involved,” says Voss, senior government affairs advisor at AAE. “And that’s not something that [the public services commission] does a good job of.”

Part of that is due to a lack of experience with water and sewer systems in general, many of which had so far been managed on the local level.

“The LPSC has not had a super long history of dealing with private water companies,” says Voss. “Water is not their primary focus. It was railroad monopolies … now it’s become electricity.”

As for ratepayers, if they lived in another state, there may be a state-funded advocate helping them pursue fair regulation of their rates. Louisiana is one of only a handful of states that don’t offer such representation.

“It’s a pretty bad time, in my view, to be a customer in Louisiana who’s hoping that the LPSC is going to protect them from what these companies want to do to them,” Voss says.

Case-Brown and Norris’ attempt to fight the rate increases on their Magnolia-issued bills failed. In June, the LPSC approved the company’s rate plan for the next three years.

But their fight, along with an increase of ratepayers across the state who find themselves in a similar situation, has brought unprecedented attention to the issue.

Magnolia will now be subject to an audit of its operating company’s finances before applying for another rate increase, ordered by the judge in Case-Brown and Norris’ intervention proceedings.

There’s also an election for the commission seat representing their area, and several candidates have made Magnolia a central part of their campaign. Norris herself is running.

Her opponent, following a recent runoff election, state Rep. Stephanie Hilferty, R-Metairie, called on the commission to stop any new rate hikes or acquisitions by Magnolia. “The residents that have Magnolia Water cannot deal with another ‘moderate’ rate hike,” she told the sitting commissioners this June.

Case-Brown, who lives in Mandeville, is proud of the work she and fellow Northshore ratepayers like Norris have done to call attention to an issue few understood or were aware of before, and against an opponent that seemed to have all the power on its side.

“We stood up to a bully and I’m proud of that,” she tells The Current. “More people need to do the same.”

title: The Next American Energy Success Story Is Already Underground - The Bully Pulpit
description:
It was 5:30 a.m. in rural Southwest Utah when I first saw what enhanced geothermal energy was really about.
The same domestic assets — the innovation, the workforce, the supply chain — that once unlocked an era of energy abundance through shale are now launching the next great American energy industry in geothermal.
True energy independence looks like an energy source secured under American land, built by American workers, and deployed with American technological expertise.
Three hundred gigawatts would make geothermal a cornerstone of American energy, representing roughly a quarter of the entire U.S. electric grid.
Tom Erb leads Federal Affairs at Fervo Energy, a leading next-generation geothermal energy company.
text:
By Tom Erb, Government Affairs & Policy Manager at Fervo

Audio playback is not supported on your browser. Please upgrade.

It was 5:30 a.m. in rural Southwest Utah when I first saw what enhanced geothermal energy was really about.

I had just started my job at Fervo Energy in September 2025 and visited Cape Station, the company’s flagship project near Milford, Utah, about 200 miles southwest of Salt Lake City. I woke up early to catch the drilling crew’s shift change and meet some of the men and women bringing a new industry to life. Standing there in the unexpectedly cold, predawn quiet, watching workers rotate out under floodlights and listening to a morning safety briefing, I was captivated by the scene: hard hats, the rumble of heavy equipment, and the organized buzz of a well-run industrial site in the high desert.

It looked like an oil and gas operation, because in many ways, it is. But what I was witnessing was something new. Fervo is building America’s next great energy industry, and it’s doing it the American way: with proven technology, a homegrown workforce, and a domestic resource that can deliver for every American, no matter what your energy priorities may be.

Innovation Built on American Expertise

Cape Station is Fervo Energy’s first commercial-scale Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) project. EGS has the potential to elevate geothermal from a niche regional resource into a backbone of reliable electricity generation across the United States, by engineering the subsurface to harvest heat from the earth and convert it into clean, reliable, affordable, and abundant power.

This is possible because EGS is built on innovations from the U.S. oil and gas sector. Fervo uses the same horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing technologies that powered the shale revolution to unlock heat stored miles beneath the Earth’s surface, bringing the same workforce and supply chain with it. More than 90 percent of on-site labor hours at Cape Station have come from oil and gas workers, and more than 60 percent of Fervo’s employees are former oil and gas professionals. The project is supplied by companies like Baker Hughes, Vallourec, and Halliburton (among others), giving Fervo confidence that equipment and resources will arrive on time via a proven domestic industrial base.

Just like with natural gas, progress is accelerating rapidly. Since 2022, Fervo has cut drilling time by approximately 75 percent and per-foot drilling costs by approximately 70 percent, mirroring the early shale revolution’s learning curve almost exactly. Cape Station is contracted to deliver first power to the grid later this year, reaching approximately 100 megawatts of operating capacity by early 2027, with permits in place to expand to 2 gigawatts. The geothermal resource beneath that single project alone exceeds 4 gigawatts, roughly equivalent to the entire traditional geothermal industry in the United States today. And Fervo’s existing lease holdings across the American West represent the potential to unlock 40 gigawatts, enough to power more than 30 million American homes.

The same domestic assets — the innovation, the workforce, the supply chain — that once unlocked an era of energy abundance through shale are now launching the next great American energy industry in geothermal.

Checking Every Box

What makes geothermal so compelling is that it checks every box, no matter what you care about most.

If you care about affordability: Americans want electricity that is both reliable and affordable. Geothermal delivers both. Cape Station’s power is already cost-competitive with other clean baseload sources, and costs are continuing to fall, driven by the same learning curve that made shale gas affordable. The market has noticed: traditional utilities and hyperscalers have signed long-term contracts to purchase geothermal power. When buyers of that caliber commit to long-term deals, it’s a signal that the economics are real and improving.

If you care about conservation and environmental impact: Geothermal produces electricity without combustion, with no fuel burned and no emissions at the source. And because the infrastructure primarily lives underground, the surface is minimally impacted. That means geothermal can deliver large-scale clean baseload power while leaving the landscape, along with the habitat, open space, and natural character that come with it, nearly untouched. Fervo’s projects run on a closed-loop water system using non-potable water sources that dramatically reduce consumption compared to conventional power plants. The projects are clean across every metric: emissions, land use, and water.

If you care about reliability: The United States faces an energy reliability crisis. Aging baseload plants are retiring faster than replacement capacity is being built, creating a potential 98-gigawatt shortfall by 2035, precisely as AI data centers, advanced manufacturing, and broad electrification are pushing demand to new heights. Geothermal produces power continuously, regardless of weather, filling the baseload gap where it’s needed most. Speed is another advantage. Fervo’s Cape Station is delivering first power in approximately three years from groundbreaking, and a modular, standardized approach is designed to shorten that timeline with every successive project.

If you care about national energy security: The heat beneath our feet cannot be embargoed, disrupted by a foreign adversary, or delayed by a pipeline failure. With EGS technology, this resource is no longer confined to Nevada and California. The Department of Energy projects geothermal opportunities in at least 18 states by 2050. True energy independence looks like an energy source secured under American land, built by American workers, and deployed with American technological expertise.

The Scale of the Opportunity

This is not a niche story. Across multiple reports and Presidential administrations, the DOE projects that the United States could deploy 90 to 300 gigawatts of geothermal power by 2050, a twentyfold increase from today. Three hundred gigawatts would make geothermal a cornerstone of American energy, representing roughly a quarter of the entire U.S. electric grid.

The Big Thing Standing in the Way

While the technology, workforce, capital, and supply chain are in a good place to scale geothermal, the single biggest bottleneck is our outdated system for permitting energy projects and building electric transmission infrastructure.

Geothermal projects on federal public lands currently face overlapping environmental reviews that the oil and gas industry is not subject to in the same way. And even after a project is permitted and built, transmission and interconnection backlogs can delay grid connection by several more years.

Both the Biden and Trump administrations have taken meaningful steps through executive action, and bipartisan legislative momentum is building. The Geothermal Energy Advancement Act and the CLEAN Act, which recently passed the House with overwhelming bipartisan support, would modernize leasing timelines, consolidate redundant reviews, and ensure agencies can keep pace with a growing industry. This is about modernizing, not eliminating, environmental review to ensure a clean, reliable, American-made energy technology isn’t unnecessarily delayed for years.

The Next Chapter

Standing at Cape Station that September morning, it’s clear I wasn’t witnessing a science experiment. I witnessed an industry being born, built by the same American workforce that built the last one, running on a resource that has been waiting underground since long before any of us were here.

The geothermal revolution can do what the shale revolution did: transform America’s energy position and provide a long-term solution to the nation’s energy affordability challenge. And it can do it while delivering for every constituency. Lower prices for ratepayers, pristine landscapes for conservationists, reliable power for grid operators, new opportunities for workers, and true energy independence for our national security. It checks every box.

What happens next depends on how many Americans are willing to put their skills, voices, and passion to work to accelerate the nation’s next great energy industry. Come join us.

Tom Erb leads Federal Affairs at Fervo Energy, a leading next-generation geothermal energy company.
